questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has a 3 day history of a painful, swollen right lower leg. She has athlete's foot between her toes. The front of the shin is red, hot and tender with an ill-defined edge. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. The left leg is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A unilateral red, hot, tender shin with an ill-defined edge and a portal of entry is cellulitis; erysipelas is sharply demarcated.

clues: red, hot and tender with an ill-defined edge
steps.x: Unilateral, poorly defined erythema with a skin break.

elim: Causes calf swelling but not a hot red tender area with fever and skin break.
Has a sharply demarcated raised edge; this edge is ill-defined.
Affects a joint, not the shin.
Bilateral, itchy and not hot or tender.

steps.x: A: Cellulitis. Poorly defined unilateral erythema = cellulitis.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has a red, hot, tender area spreading around an infected eczema patch on her forearm, with a small amount of yellow crust. Her temperature is 37.8°C. A swab of the crust grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Strep pyogenes and Staph aureus are the commonest causes; cocci in clusters means Staph aureus.

steps.x: Clusters, not chains.

elim: Gram-positive cocci in chains, not clusters.

steps.x: D: Staphylococcus aureus. Gram-positive cocci in clusters = Staph aureus.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is reviewed in the diabetes clinic. He has a BMI of 38, peripheral vascular disease, bilateral ankle oedema and dry cracked skin on his heels. He asks which infection these put him at risk of.
questions.q: Which skin infection are these features most likely to predispose him to?
questions.e: Obesity, oedema, PVD, diabetes and skin breaks all compromise the skin barrier or local perfusion, predisposing to cellulitis.

steps.x: Each feature weakens skin barrier or perfusion.

elim: Superficial and usually in children, not tied to oedema and PVD.
Viral, not linked to these risk factors.
A yeast infection, not linked to oedema.
A mite infestation, not linked to these features.

steps.x: A: Cellulitis. Obesity, oedema, PVD, diabetes, skin breaks = cellulitis risk.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man cut his finger on a fish hook 2 days ago. The finger is red, hot and swollen, and a tender red line now runs up the inside of his forearm to his elbow. His temperature is 38.2°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the red line?
questions.e: Infection spreading along superficial lymphatics towards regional nodes causes red streaking: lymphangitis.

clues: cut his finger on a fish hook
tender red line now runs up the inside of his forearm
steps.x: Red streak running towards the axilla from infection.

elim: Causes a tender cord along a vein, usually after a cannula.
Causes pain out of proportion and skin necrosis.
Itchy and not linear up the arm.
Causes limb swelling, not a red streak.

steps.x: C: Lymphangitis. Red streaking = lymphangitis.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has had cellulitis of her left thigh for 2 days. Overnight the pain has become severe and out of proportion to the skin changes, which now show dusky purple patches and crepitus. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 132 bpm and BP 88/50 mmHg.
questions.q: Which complication has most likely developed?
questions.e: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin and crepitus in a diabetic with cellulitis means necrotising fasciitis (Eron IV).

steps.x: Spread beyond subcutaneous tissue in a diabetic.

elim: Gives a fluctuant collection, not crepitus and dusky skin.
Tender nodules, not a spreading necrotic infection.

steps.x: D: Necrotising fasciitis. Pain out of proportion + crepitus = necrotising fasciitis.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with cellulitis of his right leg for 4 days has not taken his antibiotics. He is now confused with rigors. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. The leg is red without crepitus.
questions.q: Which complication has most likely developed?
questions.e: Untreated cellulitis can spread systemically, causing bacteraemia and sepsis.

steps.x: Systemic spread without features of necrosis.

elim: No severe pain on passive stretch or tense compartment.
Does not cause rigors and hypotension.
No crepitus or pain out of proportion.

steps.x: A: Bacteraemia with sepsis. Untreated cellulitis can cause bacteraemia and sepsis.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has a 2 day history of a red, warm, tender patch on his left shin after a football graze. He has no medical history. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 126/78 mmHg and respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate Eron class?
questions.e: No systemic illness and no comorbidities is Eron Class I.

steps.x: Well and no comorbidities.
A: Class I. Eron I: systemically well, no comorbidities.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and COPD has cellulitis of her right calf. She feels feverish and unwell but is alert. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate Eron class?
questions.e: Systemically unwell with comorbidities but without significant systemic upset is Eron Class IIb.

clues: feverish and unwell but is alert
steps.x: Unwell, comorbid, but stable observations.

elim: She has comorbidities and is unwell.
She is systemically unwell, not well.
No confusion, hypotension or significant tachycardia.

steps.x: C: Class IIb. Eron IIb: systemically unwell with comorbidities.

questions.stem: A 81 year old man with heart failure has cellulitis of his left leg. He is newly confused. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. There are no features of necrotising infection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate Eron class?
questions.e: Significant systemic upset (confusion, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension) is Eron Class III.

steps.x: Significant systemic upset without sepsis criteria stated.

elim: Confusion, tachycardia and tachypnoea are significant systemic upset.
Requires sepsis or necrotising fasciitis, not described.

steps.x: D: Class III. Eron III: significant systemic upset.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with severe peripheral vascular disease has cellulitis of her right foot. She feels well. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. The foot is cool with absent pulses and the toes are dusky, and the vascular team are concerned the limb is threatened.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate Eron class?
questions.e: Limb-threatening infection from vascular compromise is Eron Class III even if systemically well.

steps.x: Well, but the limb is threatened.

elim: She is not systemically unwell; limb threat defines her class.

steps.x: D: Class III. Limb-threatening infection = Eron III.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with chronic kidney disease has cellulitis of his left shin. He feels well. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 140/84 mmHg and respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate Eron class?
questions.e: Systemically well with a comorbidity is Eron Class IIa; Class IV is sepsis or necrotising fasciitis.

steps.x: Well, but with a comorbidity.

elim: No systemic upset or limb threat.
Reserved for sepsis or necrotising fasciitis.

steps.x: B: Class IIa. Eron IIa: well with a comorbidity.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has a 2 day history of a red, hot, tender area on her left calf after a cat scratch on her ankle. She is systemically well. Her temperature is 37.3°C and pulse rate 76 bpm. The GP is confident of the diagnosis.
questions.q: How is the diagnosis best confirmed?
questions.e: Cellulitis is a clinical diagnosis made on history and examination alone.

steps.x: Typical features, well patient.

elim: Only if severe infection is suspected.
Not routine; for suspected deep infection.

steps.x: B: Clinically on history and examination. Cellulitis is diagnosed clinically.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is admitted with cellulitis of his right leg. He is uncomfortable. His temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. The team sends routine bloods.
questions.q: Which is the most likely result?
questions.e: Blood tests in cellulitis show a raised CRP and raised WCC.

steps.x: Bacterial infection with fever.

elim: Non-specific and not the expected finding.

steps.x: C: Raised CRP and raised WCC. Raised CRP and WCC.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman with cellulitis of her left leg is drowsy with rigors. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 90/54 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. IV access has been obtained.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting antibiotics?
questions.e: Blood cultures are taken when severe infection is suspected, before antibiotics.

steps.x: Severe systemic infection.
A: Blood cultures. Blood cultures if severe cellulitis is suspected.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with suspected cellulitis of her right forearm is seen in the GP surgery. She is alert, temperature 37.6°C and pulse rate 84 bpm. She asks whether she needs a scan or swab before treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to investigation?
questions.e: Cellulitis is clinical; bloods (CRP, WCC) and cultures are reserved for more severe cases.

clues: a scan or swab before treatment
steps.x: Well patient with a typical picture.

elim: She is well, so not indicated.
Not useful when skin is unbroken.

steps.x: D: No investigation needed before treatment. Treat on clinical diagnosis; tests only if severe.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has a 2 day history of a red, hot, tender right shin after a graze. He has no allergies and no medical history. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate dose of the first-line antibiotic?
o: Amoxicillin 250 mg once daily for 3 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 14 days
Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times a day for 5 to 7 days
Flucloxacillin 500 mg once daily for 1 day
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 3 days
questions.e: First-line for Eron I cellulitis is oral flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS for 5 to 7 days (NICE NG141).

clues: no allergies and no medical history
steps.x: Well, no allergy, Eron I.
C: Flucloxacillin 500 mg four times a day for 5 to 7 days. Flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS, 5 to 7 days.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman started oral flucloxacillin yesterday for cellulitis of her left lower leg. She is well. She asks what else she can do at home to help the leg settle.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional advice?
o: Elevate the leg and take analgesia
questions.e: Supportive care is elevation of the affected limb and analgesia.

clues: what else she can do at home
steps.x: Antibiotics started; she wants supportive measures.
C: Elevate the leg and take analgesia. Elevate the limb and give analgesia.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has cellulitis of his right forearm. He had anaphylaxis to penicillin as a child. He is systemically well with a temperature of 37.5°C and pulse rate 84 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: In true penicillin allergy use a macrolide such as clarithromycin (or doxycycline or clindamycin).

steps.x: True penicillin allergy.
B: Clarithromycin. Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin, doxycycline or clindamycin.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 18 weeks pregnant has cellulitis of her left shin after a scratch. She developed a widespread urticarial rash with amoxicillin last year. She is systemically well with a temperature of 37.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Pregnancy with penicillin allergy: oral erythromycin.

steps.x: Pregnant and truly penicillin allergic.

elim: Avoid in early pregnancy and wrong spectrum.

steps.x: C: Oral erythromycin. Pregnancy plus penicillin allergy = erythromycin.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has cellulitis of his left leg. His notes record a penicillin allergy. On questioning, he had mild nausea and loose stools when he took amoxicillin for a chest infection 2 years ago, with no rash or swelling.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Diarrhoea and nausea with amoxicillin are common side effects, not true allergy, so first-line flucloxacillin is appropriate.

steps.x: An intolerance, not an allergy.

elim: Not needed; this is not a true allergy.
Not needed and increases C. difficile risk.

steps.x: E: Oral flucloxacillin. GI upset is a side effect, not penicillin allergy.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with type 2 diabetes was bitten on the hand by her neighbour's cat 36 hours ago. The hand is now red, hot and swollen around two puncture wounds. She has no allergies. Her temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 90 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely organism to cover with antibiotics?
questions.e: Cat bites transmit Pasteurella multocida; oral co-amoxiclav is first-line to cover it.

clues: bitten on the hand by her neighbour's cat
steps.x: A cat bite.

elim: Tetanus is prevented by vaccination, not the cause of cellulitis.

steps.x: D: Pasteurella multocida. Cat bite = Pasteurella; co-amoxiclav.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with diabetes has rapidly spreading cellulitis of his right thigh with pain out of proportion and early skin blistering. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. IV ceftriaxone has been started.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Severe cellulitis needs IV antibiotics plus urgent surgical review to exclude necrotising fasciitis.

steps.x: Possible necrotising infection already on IV antibiotics.
E: Urgent surgical consultation. Severe cellulitis: IV antibiotics plus urgent surgery review.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has sepsis from cellulitis of her right leg. She has received IV co-amoxiclav and IV fluids. A nasal swab from a recent admission grew MRSA, and today's blood cultures grow MRSA. Her BP is 102/64 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to her antibiotics?
questions.e: Sepsis from cellulitis is treated with IV co-amoxiclav and fluids, switching to IV vancomycin if MRSA is suspected or confirmed.

steps.x: Confirmed MRSA bacteraemia.
D: Switch to IV vancomycin. MRSA: switch to IV vancomycin.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with heart failure has cellulitis of his left leg. He is newly confused, with a temperature of 38.7°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 100/60 mmHg. He has no allergies and no features of necrotising infection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oral clarithromycin and metronidazole at home
questions.e: Severe infection (Eron III) needs hospital admission and IV flucloxacillin; oral second-line regimens are for milder disease.

steps.x: Severe systemic upset without allergy.

elim: Second-line oral regimen; he needs admission.

steps.x: A: Admit for IV flucloxacillin. Severe cellulitis: admit for IV flucloxacillin.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has a red, warm, swollen, tender area on her left calf 2 days after a gardening scratch. A student asks what causes the redness and swelling.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Acute inflammation with vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
questions.e: Bacteria invade the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, triggering vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and neutrophil recruitment, giving erythema, warmth and swelling.

steps.x: An acute infection after a skin break.

elim: Causes swelling without heat and tenderness.
Causes chronic swelling, not acute inflammation.

steps.x: A: Acute inflammation with vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. Acute inflammation causes the red, hot, swollen skin.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has cellulitis around an insect bite on his ankle. The swab grows beta-haemolytic Gram-positive cocci in chains that are Lancefield group A.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus, Strep pyogenes, is the most common cause of cellulitis.

steps.x: Group A beta-haemolytic chains.
E: Streptococcus pyogenes. Strep pyogenes: commonest cause of cellulitis.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with obesity and chronic lymphoedema of both legs has her third episode of cellulitis this year, each taking longer to settle. A student asks why she is predisposed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Impaired local perfusion and lymphatic drainage
questions.e: Obesity, oedema and vascular disease impair perfusion and lymphatic drainage, predisposing to invasion and slowing resolution.

steps.x: Recurrent, slow-to-resolve infection with lymphoedema.
B: Impaired local perfusion and lymphatic drainage. Poor perfusion and drainage predispose and slow healing.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with poorly controlled diabetes and on long-term prednisolone develops cellulitis that progresses within 24 hours to necrosis of the deep fascia. A student asks why he was at particular risk.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Impaired immunity allowing spread beyond the subcutaneous tissue
questions.e: In immunocompromised or diabetic patients bacteria can invade beyond the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, causing necrotising fasciitis or sepsis.

steps.x: Two causes of impaired immunity.

elim: Does not cause spread of infection.

steps.x: C: Impaired immunity allowing spread beyond the subcutaneous tissue. Immunocompromise lets cellulitis spread deeper.
